batch_name: Ouroboros: Unity of Matter in Alchemy
description: Concept entry for the Ouroboros (serpent devouring its tail), the central symbol of Greek alchemy representing the unity of matter, the cyclic nature of the alchemical work, and the principle of self-transformation. Based on H. J. Sheppard, 'The Ouroboros and the Unity of Matter in Alchemy: A Study in Origins,' Ambix 10:2 (1962) pp.83-96; and H. J. Sheppard, 'Gnosticism and Alchemy,' Ambix 6:2 (1957) pp.86-101.

concepts.label: Ouroboros
concepts.definition_long:
The Ouroboros (from Greek oura, 'tail' + boros, 'devouring') — a serpent or dragon depicted in the act of devouring its own tail — is one of the most ancient and widespread symbols in Greek and later European alchemy, where it principally signified the unity of matter, the cyclic and endless character of the alchemical work, and the capacity of matter to transform and regenerate itself. In the alchemical context the Ouroboros carried the inscription hen to pan (One is the All), tracing the principle of unity-in-diversity from the pre-Socratic philosopher Xenophanes of Colophon (ca. 570–460 BCE) through Stoic natural philosophy and Gnostic cosmology into the practical-mystical framework of Hellenistic alchemy. H. J. Sheppard, in Ambix (1962), traces the symbol's origin from ancient Egyptian cosmogony — the Pyramid Texts of the 6th Dynasty (ca. 2350–2250 BCE) depict a 'Provider of Attributes serpent with its many coils' as the creative spirit giving essence to all things — and follows it through Babylonian astrology (draco caelestis, the celestial dragon of the Chaldaeans), Gnostic serpent symbolism (particularly the Ophite and Valentinian sects), and apocryphal Christian texts before it appears in the alchemical tradition.

The earliest alchemical occurrence of the Ouroboros appears in the Chrysopoeia (Gold-Making) of Kleopatra (ca. 3rd–4th century CE), preserved in the Greek alchemical manuscript Marcianus 299 (folio 188v), where a simple serpent-devouring-its-tail figure bears the inscription hen to pan in its centre. A more elaborate version in the same manuscript consists of three concentric circles enclosing the planetary symbols for gold, silver, and mercury, with the outer ring bearing the inscription 'One is All and through it is All, and to it All, and if it has not All, All is nothing' and the inner ring 'One is the Serpent having its venom according to two compositions' — the 'two compositions' referring to the sulphur-mercury duality of alchemical theory. In the Visions of Zosimos of Panopolis (ca. 300 CE), the Ouroboros symbolizes the sacrificial and regenerative dimension of the alchemical work: a priest undergoes death, dismemberment, and transformation into spirit (pneuma), in an exact parallel with the self-devouring serpent, which C. G. Jung analyzed as representing the unity of the prima and ultima materia in alchemy. In later Latin and vernacular alchemy the Ouroboros image was also assimilated to the Green Dragon or 'Green Lion' and to the killing and revivification of metals in the alchemical opus, as in the sixth parable of the Splendor Solis and Michael Maier's Atalanta Fugiens (1617). Sheppard, in Ambix (1957), argues that the Gnostic serpent symbolism — particularly the Ophites' identification of the serpent with Christ, the principle of pneuma, and the circle of outer darkness surrounding the world (Pistis Sophia) — was directly adopted by alchemists working in Hellenistic Alexandria, producing the characteristically dual, simultaneously material and spiritual, quality of alchemical symbolism that pervades Western alchemy through the Renaissance and beyond.
